facts.statement: Charactosuchus was assigned to the family Crocodylidae in 1988.
facts.quote: It was assigned to the family Crocodylidae in 1988.

facts.statement: Fossils of Charactosuchus have been found in Colombia, Brazil, Jamaica, and possibly Florida and South Carolina.
facts.quote: Specimens have been found in Colombia, Brazil, Jamaica, and possibly Florida and South Carolina.

facts.statement: The type species C. fieldsi lived during the Middle Miocene in the Villavieja Formation at La Venta, Colombia.
facts.quote: The type species, C. fieldsi, has been found from the Villavieja Formation at the Konzentrat-Lagerstätte La Venta in Colombia and dates back to the Middle Miocene (Laventan).

facts.statement: Charactosuchus fossils have been found in the Urumaco Formation in Venezuela and the Solimões Formation in Brazil.
facts.quote: It has also been found in the Mayoan to Montehermosan Urumaco Formation at Urumaco in Venezuela, and in the Solimões Formation in Acre State, Brazil, along with C. sansoai, and the possible species C. mendesi (sometimes assigned to Brasilosuchus).

facts.statement: A lower jaw dated to the Lutetian stage of the Eocene found in Jamaica was described as the species C. kugleri in 1969.
facts.quote: In 1969, a lower jaw of a crocodilian that dated back to the Lutetian stage of the Eocene was found in the Chapelton Formation of Saint James Parish, Jamaica, and was described as belonging to a new species of Charactosuchus named C. kugleri.

facts.statement: It is debated whether C. kugleri is a valid species or a synonym of Dollosuchus.
facts.quote: However, this species may be considered synonymous with Dollosuchus, according to later papers.

facts.statement: Isolated teeth attributed to Charactosuchus from Florida and South Carolina date to the early Pliocene.
facts.quote: Isolated teeth thought to be from the genus have been found from Florida and South Carolina and are of early Pliocene age.

facts.statement: The theory that Charactosuchus migrated from North America to South America is no longer accepted, while its presence in Jamaica suggests a possible European origin via land bridges.
facts.quote: This theory is no longer accepted, although the presence of Charactosuchus from Jamaica may suggest a European origin, with the genus migrating across either the De Geer or Thule land bridges.

facts.statement: Charactosuchus has been classified within the families Crocodylidae and Gavialidae.
Charactosuchus has been placed in the subfamily Tomistominae.
The precise classification of Charactosuchus depends on the controversy regarding the placement of the subfamily Tomistominae within the order Crocodylia.
facts.quote: aunque su asignación precisa depende de la controversia sobre la relación de la subfamilia Tomistominae (que incluye al moderno falso gavial, Tomistoma) dentro del orden Crocodylia.

facts.statement: Charactosuchus lived from the Lutetian to the Tortonian stages, approximately 48.07 to 7.246 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Lutetian to Tortonian (48.07 to 7.246 million years ago)

rejected.statement: Charactosuchus had a long, narrow snout resembling a gharial but was more closely related to modern crocodiles than to gharials.
rejected.quote: It was gharial-like in appearance with its long narrow snout but bore no relation to them, being more closely related to modern crocodiles than to gharials.
